title: Orionid Meteor Shower: Halley's Dust, 66 km/s #Shorts
description:
Orionid meteor shower 2026: what you're seeing is Halley's Comet dust, hitting our sky at 66 kilometres per second, about 260 times faster than a passenger jet. Each grain is about the size of a grain of sand, yet at that speed it vaporises around 100 kilometres up and the air around it glows. The peak was on 21 October, but the shower runs until about 22 November, so there's still a chance to catch a streak of dust Halley shed long ago.
New Sky This Week episodes every week. Subscribe for more hopeful science, and tell us where you spotted one.
Sources: EarthSky Orionids 2026 guide; CNN (21 Oct 2026); Natural History Museum.
Footage: stock clips for illustration (Pixabay, NASA), not of the actual event.
#Shorts #space #science #Orionids #HalleysComet

script:
SKY THIS WEEK, EP.1. Short 9:16, ~48s. Time-sensitive: "fewer, not zero" and "next few weeks" hold only until ~22 Nov 2026.

HOOK 0:00-0:04 ARJUN (on camera): "Sixty-six kilometres per second. That's how fast an Orionid meteor hits our sky. So how can a grain of sand light it up?"
ANSWER 0:04-0:10 ARJUN (VO): "Speed. At that speed the grain vaporises about a hundred kilometres up, and the air around it glows. That's the streak."
BEAT1 0:10-0:17 MEERA (VO): "Each October, Earth ploughs through the trail of dust left by Halley's Comet. The grains are tiny, about the size of a grain of sand."
BEAT2 0:17-0:27 ARJUN (VO): "Halley gives us two showers a year, the Orionids now and the Eta Aquariids in May. It last passed in 1986 and returns in 2061. The dust it shed long ago still drifts along its orbit, so we cross it every year."
BEAT3 0:27-0:36 MEERA (VO): "The peak was 21 October. Under ideal dark skies you'd see up to about twenty an hour. A bright moon washed out the evening, but it set before dawn and left a dark window."
BEAT4 0:36-0:43 MEERA (VO): "Rates fall off through November, so expect fewer, not zero. Try after moonset and before dawn, with a clear dark sky."
SIGN-OFF 0:43-0:48 ARJUN (on camera): "Many of the streaks you see in the next few weeks are Halley's dust. Where did you spot one? Tell us. Subscribe to Sky This Week."

CAST: Arjun (host, fixed reference look, rooftop at night, on camera at hook/shot 11/sign-off, calm curious voice); Meera (VO beats 1,3,4); Lumen (silent stock B-roll Indian student: nod/smile at "Halley's dust" ~0:15, looks up ~0:41).
